editor_spans.body: Underneath the government's Ukraine statements this week is a domestic worry about energy prices. The Prime Minister did not present the energy ceasefire mainly as a way to protect Ukrainians. He presented it as "the quickest way" to get diesel "back onto world markets". The 9 October response to the US–Russia agreement stopped to note the effect on "energy prices and the cost of living". The Chancellor opened his IMF remarks with conflict in the Middle East and Europe "hitting people across the world".

That explains why the diplomacy happened in the order it did. London welcomed Washington's reciprocal energy ceasefire within a day and had Kyiv pledge to apply it at once. Only after Russian strikes continued did London fall back on missiles and sanctions. The phrase "standing by plans" for the LNG shipping-services ban is a tell. Governments don't announce that they are keeping a policy unless someone has suggested dropping it, and the obvious reason to drop it is cheaper gas. Expect that pull to grow over the winter.

Look at the numbers as well. The "double down" headline rests on bringing forward £10 million of a £45 million missile package. The existing commitment is £1.6 billion over four years. Sanctions, military aid and fiscal support are only being "drawn up". So far this is mostly about timing, not new money, and readers should check whether real packages actually arrive "in the coming weeks".

The rail HQ announcement and the Scotland speech, a day apart, follow the same idea. The Prime Minister made his name as a city-region mayor, and he is now governing with a mayor's instincts. That means moving institutions out of the capital and telling Holyrood to pass power down too. The Derby HQ and the Lanarkshire speech both say young people should not "have to move away". The Scotland offer is about "regions and cities" driving "reindustrialisation".

In Scotland, though, the offer is also a political move. Calling the Scottish Government "one of the most centralised devolved administrations in Europe" turns the old argument around: Westminster now claims to be the decentraliser. Local government is devolved to Holyrood, so nothing named in the speech can happen unless Edinburgh agrees, and no mechanism is set out. Under "two governments, one goal", Labour is setting up an argument about centralisation in Edinburgh, aimed at the next Holyrood contest.

The Derby announcement deserves some scepticism too. Derby was already chosen to host GBR in 2023, under the previous government. What is new is a building, finishing in spring 2029, for up to 450 staff. Many of those staff are likely to move from existing bodies rather than fill new jobs. The more lasting finding is buried lower down: fewer than 7% of rail workers are under 25. The industry's real long-term problem is an ageing workforce, and 600 apprentices over four years is a modest answer to it.

The biggest item in the Commons statement got little attention. Beyond the 20 November summit, the Prime Minister proposed "a serious dialogue about the different options" for Britain's long-term relationship with the EU. He said "the British public will be the boss", and he called the status quo a "dereliction of duty". That is the first time since the 2016 settlement that a government has formally opened the question of the relationship as a whole. Saying the public will be "the boss" points towards an eventual public vote. How carefully he worded it shows how much political risk he thinks it carries.

The case he made is mostly about the costs of trade friction at the border: 100% document checks on Scottish salmon, export health certificates, seed potatoes and shellfish shut out. He picked Scottish and Welsh examples on purpose. That links the EU case to the push for the regions and the devolved nations, and explains why the summit's benefits were described place by place, down to Northern Ireland's energy costs.
